stories.title: The Deer Hunt
stories.description: Amit uses the analogy of a prehistoric tribe hunting a deer to explain the evolutionary origin of the Zero-Sum Fallacy: in that context, if one person took a piece of meat, another couldn't have it.

stories.title: Ryan's Penance
stories.description: Amit shares a college anecdote about his friend Ryan, who did 25 push-ups every time he 'sinned' (masturbated). Another friend, observing Ryan's muscular physique, wrongly concluded that masturbation causes muscle growth (Post Hoc Ergo Propter Hoc).

stories.title: The Witch Doctor and the Nile
stories.description: Ajay tells a story about a witch doctor who claims that taking off his coat causes the Nile to flood, illustrating the difficulty of establishing true causality.

stories.title: Canteen vs. Tapri
stories.description: Amit describes his college dilemma of choosing between the canteen and the tapri based on the wind direction, to avoid his ribs showing through his shirt because he was so thin.

recommendations.comment: Thomas Sowell's book, which serves as the framework for the episode.
Robert Axelrod's book on game theory and cooperation.
Chris Blattman's book on the roots of violence and war.
Arnold Kling's book on how different political tribes speak different languages (Liberty, Equality, Civilization).
Sowell's analysis (and Amity Shlaes' book) arguing that government intervention, not the stock market crash, caused the Great Depression.
Michael Crichton's phrase describing the confusion of cause and effect.

core_ideas.description: The instinctive belief that one person's gain must be another's loss. In reality, voluntary trade is positive-sum (the 'double thank you' moment).
The belief that what is true for a part is true for the whole. Example: One farmer growing tomatoes makes money; all farmers doing it causes a glut.
The fallacy of assuming that because X happened before Y, X caused Y. Correlation does not imply causation.
The arrogant belief (Fatal Conceit) that a leader can move people around like chess pieces to achieve a desired outcome, ignoring their individual agency and spontaneous order.
The belief that resources are unlimited and can be spent on every good cause without trade-offs. In reality, resources are limited and have alternative uses.

core_ideas.item: Pessimism of the Intellect, Optimism of the Will
core_ideas.description: Gramsci's quote, cited by Amit as a way to approach the world's problems.

Ajay's reference to how random stock picking often beats experts.
